query: Consider the following context: Refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered promising candidate materials for next‐generation nuclear reactors due to their superior mechanical strength, irradiation resistance, and thermal stability at high temperatures. However, the significant positive heat of mixing between refractory alloying elements and Cu, commonly used in cooling systems, poses challenges in forming composite structures. In that context, which method can be used for large‐scale reaction and stable microstructure, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Utilizing an advanced free-energy sampling method, such as metadynamics, during thermal processing of RHEA-Cu composites enables a self-sustaining, large-scale reaction that leads to a stable, homogeneous microstructure by overcoming the inherent thermodynamic demixing due to positive heat of mixing.
generation.material_initial_state: A precursor composite mixture of refractory high-entropy alloy elements and copper, which is predisposed to phase segregation because of the significant positive heat of mixing between the refractory elements and Cu.
generation.intervention: During high-temperature processing, implement an advanced sampling method (e.g., metadynamics) to explore and navigate the free energy landscape, thereby triggering reaction pathways that bypass demixing barriers.
generation.conditions: Controlled high-temperature conditions with real-time monitoring of reaction progress, ensuring sufficient thermal energy to allow the system to sample alternative reaction pathways while mitigating phase segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: The development of transient, metastable phases and nucleation sites as the free energy barriers are overcome, which mediate the formation of a homogeneous composite microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Metadynamics drives the reaction system through free energy barriers, identifying and stabilizing favorable processing windows that allow the refractory elements and copper to react cohesively rather than segregate. This targeted sampling of the free energy landscape reduces the kinetic and thermodynamic penalties associated with the positive heat of mixing.
generation.predicted_outcome: The composite will form a large-scale, uniform microstructure with reduced phase segregation, leading to enhanced structural stability under high-temperature and irradiation conditions typical of next-generation nuclear reactors.
generation.baseline: Without advanced sampling, traditional processing methods result in significant phase segregation and unstable microstructures due to the high positive heat of mixing between Cu and the refractory elements.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to work effectively when processing conditions allow adequate free energy sampling and when the kinetics of diffusion are not prohibitively slow; the method’s efficacy might be limited if intrinsic diffusion rates or other extrinsic factors (e.g., processing scale) prevent the full exploitation of the optimized reaction pathway.
generation.uncertainty: The specific processing parameters (temperature profiles, timing, cooling rates) required to consistently achieve the optimized microstructure are not precisely defined. It is also uncertain how well the method scales from lab-scale experiments to industrial-scale composite production.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of RHEA-Cu composite samples under identical initial conditions. Process one set with a metadynamics-informed thermal treatment protocol and the other set with a conventional thermal treatment protocol. Monitor the reaction and microstructural evolution in real time using in situ characterization tools.
measurements: Phase composition analysis using X-ray diffraction (XRD)
Microstructural characterization via scanning/transmission electron microscopy (SEM/TEM)
Mechanical property evaluation (e.g., compression tests, hardness measurements)
Thermal stability and irradiation resistance tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples processed with the metadynamics-informed protocol do not show a statistically significant improvement (increased homogeneity, reduced phase segregation, and enhanced mechanical and thermal stability) over the baseline samples processed conventionally, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ].
